title: Limits of online selection with a fixed number of choices
shortTitle: How close can online choices get to hindsight?
oneLine: An unrefereed mathematical candidate characterises the long-horizon worst-case ratio for every fixed selection budget and certifies a narrow interval near 83.7% for two choices.
abstract: For independent, identically distributed nonnegative observations from a known law with finite positive mean, an online decision maker may accept at most k values. This candidate proves existence of the worst-case optimal-online-to-top-k-prophet ratio as the horizon tends to infinity, for each fixed positive integer k, and identifies it with a continuum minimax value. Written transfer and compactness arguments cover the general theorem. For k=2, explicit policy and value-profile witnesses certified with Arb give 0.83695 <= gamma_2* <= 0.8372914, within the rounded headline interval [0.83695, 0.83730]. A separate certified comparison establishes asymptotic non-tightness of the specified earlier nonlinear-system value. No equality with the infimum over all horizons, exact constant, uniform-in-k rate, or numerical certificate for k>=3 is claimed.

keyResults: For each fixed positive integer k, the worst-case optimal-online/top-k-prophet ratio has a limit as the number of observations grows.
The limit equals a continuum profile infimum and a compact cumulative-coverage game maximum; this does not assert attainment by a bounded policy or worst-case profile.
For two selections, the supplied certified witnesses give [0.83695, 0.8372914], and hence the rounded interval [0.83695, 0.83730].
The specified earlier two-unit nonlinear-system value is strictly below this asymptotic constant; the all-horizon infimum question remains separate.
An occupancy-weighted threshold construction dominates finite policy mixtures; this is attributed to established occupancy/flow principles, not claimed as a new purification principle.

narration: How close can online choices get to hindsight? An Evidence Press audio briefing. Imagine seeing a sequence of offers, one at a time. You know the probability distribution, but you cannot see the next offer. Once you reject an offer, it is gone. You may accept at most a fixed number of them. A prophet, by contrast, sees the whole sequence and takes the best offers. The question is how much of the prophet's expected total an optimal online strategy can guarantee, even for the hardest distribution. The offers must be independent draws from the same known distribution, with nonnegative values and a finite positive average. This research candidate proves that, for every fixed number of allowed choices, the worst-case ratio approaches a limit as the sequence becomes longer. It characterises that limit by balancing selection strategies against difficult value distributions. For two choices, certified bounds put the limit between eighty-three point six nine five percent and eighty-three point seven three zero percent. This is a narrow interval, not an exact constant, and not a promise for every finite sequence length. The proof connects a continuous-time model back to finite sequences. Explicit strategy and distribution witnesses are checked using arithmetic that bounds rounding errors. The work also shows that one earlier two-choice lower-bound construction does not reach the asymptotic optimum. It does not settle the worst ratio over all sequence lengths or provide new numerical constants for larger selection budgets. This is AI-assisted, unrefereed mathematics, not a study of real purchasing or hiring decisions. The manuscript and checking materials are the route to inspecting the evidence. This briefing accompanies the fifteenth of October twenty twenty-six candidate on iid multi-unit prophet limits. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
